analysis.one_liner: Requires cable companies to stop scrambling basic channels and disclose converter box limits to customers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred cable companies from scrambling basic cable channels and required them to tell customers when a converter box disables features of their own TV or VCR, like taping one show while watching another. It would also have forced cable operators to offer direct hookups at their own expense, let customers buy remotes anywhere instead of renting, and required new TVs of 13 inches or larger to come with a built-in port for descramblers.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, especially the growing share who owned "cable ready" televisions and VCRs in the early 1990s. They would keep full use of features they paid for when buying their TV — picture-in-picture, timer recording of two shows on different channels — instead of losing those features to a cable company's converter box. Customers renting remotes from their cable company would learn they could buy one anywhere, and the ban on scrambling basic cable would mean the channels everyone already paid for arrived unencrypted, ready to plug straight into a TV.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers with cable-ready TVs and VCRs

how_it_helps.text: Bars cable operators from scrambling or encrypting any signal offered as part of basic cable service, so the channels subscribers already pay for arrive unencrypted and usable on any TV or VCR without extra equipment [S3].

Requires cable companies to warn subscribers that delivery through a converter box can disable features of their own TV or VCR — like watching one channel while taping another, taping consecutive shows on different channels, or picture-in-picture [S3].

Requires operators to offer, at the cable company's expense, to install or reinstall service so that channels not needing a converter box go directly into the subscriber's cable-ready television or VCR [S2, S3].

Requires cable companies renting out remote controls to tell customers they may buy a remote from any source, list compatible models, and prohibits operators from disabling their converter boxes' compatibility with store-bought remotes [S2, S3].

Directs the FCC to require all new televisions with screens of 13 inches or larger sold in the U.S. to include multiport technology, and requires cable operators to replace converter boxes with compatible descrambling units at their own expense for subscribers with such TVs — permanently ending the converter-box toll on future TV purchases [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable television operators, who would absorb the cost of scrambled-signal restrictions, free reinstallations, descrambler unit replacements, and the loss of rental income from remote controls and converter boxes. Television manufacturers would bear the cost of building multiport technology into every new set of 13 inches or larger. Those costs could be passed to subscribers through rates, though the bill aimed to reduce the equipment customers had to rent in the first place.

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on cable operators and TV manufacturers, and cable operators could have recouped them through higher subscription rates, so some of the benefit might have come back to subscribers as a price increase [S3].

The ban on scrambling basic cable service could have complicated cable operators' ability to manage their systems or control signal theft on basic tiers, a trade-off the bill acknowledged by confining the ban to basic service only [S3].

Mandating multiport technology in every TV of 13 inches or larger sold in the United States imposed a manufacturing requirement whose timing the FCC would have to set, raising the risk of forcing TV makers to build in hardware that some systems would never use [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit was real but modest: easier use of TVs and VCRs people already owned, more honest disclosure, and the end of forced renting of remotes and converter boxes over time. The cost — absorbed by cable operators and TV makers, and possibly partly passed through in rates — was also modest. It was a consumer-protection bill of the everyday-convenience kind, not a measure with large dollar stakes, and it was narrowly drawn enough (keeping the scrambling ban to basic service, leaving timing to the FCC) that it posed little risk of serious side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Leahy introduced the Cable Ready Equipment Act of 1991 on November 26, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1, S5].
The Commerce Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators kept the status quo: they could continue scrambling basic service, renting converter boxes and remote controls, and installing service through converter boxes that disabled features of subscribers' own TVs and VCRs. TV makers faced no multiport mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators, unaffected by the rules

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the Cable Ready Equipment Act of 1991

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never held a hearing or markup, letting it die at the end of the 102nd Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors and no recorded vote, so no party alignment was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill would have ended scrambling of basic service, forced free reinstallations and descrambler replacements for cable-ready TV owners, and cut into rental revenue from converter boxes and remote controls. Its death left cable operators' equipment-rental business model untouched.

Manufacturers would have had to build multiport technology into every new TV of 13 inches or larger, a compliance cost — but their 'cable ready' sets would finally work as advertised instead of being sidelined by converter boxes, which could have made those features a selling point.
